AlternateTargets: a monk living on communal meals
Senses.Explanation: A gruel-and-rice monk is an ordinary monastery resident living within the community's daily support. Chan records use the same human role in self-description, refusal of public office, prohibition, contrast, and vow; those appraisals do not turn the resident into different kinds of person. Fenyang Shanzhao, repeatedly summoned to prestigious monasteries, says, “I am a long-term gruel-and-rice monk; transmitting the buddha-mind lineage is no small matter” (我長行粥飯僧，傳佛心宗非細事也) and refuses eight invitations. Huaiyu Xuan Shouzuo declines Nanyuan by saying that he has long been a gruel-and-rice monk and will not emerge into the human world. Baoci Guangyun simply identifies himself as one. In contrastive uses, an official asks whether Weishan Lingyou's assembly consists of monks who eat gruel and rice or monks who investigate Chan; Weishan repeats and rejects both categories. Zhenjing Kewen warns the assembly not to become long-term gruel-and-rice monks. Xiangyan Zhixian says he will stop studying the buddha teaching and become one, sparing his mind the labor, while Puming's verse joins the same role to ceasing pursuit of learned knowledge yet insisting on clarifying mind. The Zen bend lies in making ordinary communal subsistence a public identity and test. Approval, self-deprecation, refusal, and rebuke are readings of one role, not separate senses.
Senses.Note: The headword has 59 hits in 42 allowlisted texts. The earlier two-sense split was rejected on independent review: institutional residence and being characterized by the meals that support it do not establish incompatible referents. The exact same long-term gruel-and-rice-monk form occurs in refusal and admonition contexts, proving that appraisal and surrounding contrast cannot define separate senses. Related food and insult terms remain lexically distinct and do not donate stronger meanings to this compound.
